Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
I've read it. Here is a summary of the comment, my assessment of each section, and where the evidence now stands across all three papers.

## What the comment says

Using the Halden microdata, the authors make four corrections:

- **Attrition:** seven of the nine withdrawals happened *after* the schedule began, mostly citing workload. The working paper described them as preparation-phase withdrawals for scheduling reasons.
- **Output measure:** in 23 organisations with submitted records, manager-reported output exceeded record-based output by 3.8 points, and it did so in 19 of the 23.
- **Hours:** time-tracking in 27 organisations shows actual hours fell 14.1%, not 20%.
- **Revenue:** deflated by 4.1% CPI, the 1.4% nominal rise becomes a real fall of about 2.6%.

In the 17 organisations with both records and time-tracking, the per-hour gain falls from 23.4% to 10.8%.

The comment then argues three further things:
- The residual is plausibly novelty, citing the energy decline from 0.61 to 0.29 SD.
- The Varden meetings finding is post hoc and should not be cited.
- Per-hour gains from reduced hours are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty."

## Overall assessment

The comment has two halves of very different weight:

- **Sections 1–5 are strong.** They are empirical corrections from the primary data, and they substantially revise the Halden result. They should be taken at full weight.
- **Sections 6–8 go well beyond the evidence.** The conclusion that the gains are "entirely an artifact" is contradicted by the strongest study available, which is the one the comment itself praises.

I checked the arithmetic:

| Calculation | Result | Holds? |
|---|---|---|
| 95.1 / 0.8 | +18.9% | ✓ |
| 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% | ✓ |
| 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% | ✓ |
| Hours ratios 34.6/40.3 and 34.8/40.4 | | ✓ |
| Real revenue: 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% | ✓ |

Two exceptions are noted below.

## Sections 1–5: the corrections

**Attrition (§1) is the most important finding in the comment.** It shows that the working paper misdescribed when and why organisations withdrew, which is a factual error in the original, not just a matter of interpretation. Halden should issue a correction.

The comment doesn't quantify the effect, though. It also recommends analysing all enrolled organisations without doing so itself. If any outcome data exist for the withdrawers, even one or two months, an intention-to-treat estimate or a simple bound would help. For example: what would the headline become if the nine organisations had output of 85? That would turn "a sample of survivors" into a number.

Minor: "six of the nine gave workload… and two gave scheduling" accounts for eight. What did the ninth give?

**The output measure (§2) is well evidenced.** A systematic gap of 19 out of 23 is hard to explain as noise. Two refinements:
- Say whether the Table 1 means are employee-weighted like Halden's, so the two are comparable.
- Organisations that submitted records may differ from those that didn't. The Data note acknowledges this.

**The hours decomposition (§3) doesn't add up.** Consider the components the comment reports:
- Days 0.7 hours longer on four days adds 2.8 hours.
- Plus 1.6 hours logged on the day off.
- That gives about 36.4 hours per week, not the reported 34.6.

Either the +0.7 figure or the 34.6 figure is wrong. If 36.4 is right, the hours ratio is about 0.90 and the corrected gain shrinks further, to around 9%. So the error may cut in the authors' favour, but it needs resolving.

**Table 2 changes the sample between rows.** The rows use 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations. Each step therefore mixes the effect of the correction with a change in which organisations are included. Running all four specifications on the same 17 organisations would show what each correction does on its own.

**Revenue (§4) is correct.** It confirms the inflation point I raised about the Halden paper. CPI is a rough deflator for these firms' prices, but the direction is clearly right.

**Sectors (§5) is correct on the metric.** "Any index above 80 registers a gain" is the same point I made earlier, and the record-based retail figure of −11.2% strengthens it. That figure rests on three organisations, though.

**One consequence the comment doesn't draw out:** in the corrected subset, output per *employee* was 95.4, so output per employee fell by about 5%. For employers, that is arguably the more decision-relevant correction.

## Sections 6–8: where the comment overreaches

**1. The conclusion contradicts the strongest evidence the comment cites.**
The Varden case-processing stratum estimated a +12.5% gain per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4). That trial addresses each of the three proposed sources of artifact:
- **Measurement:** output came from administrative records and hours from timesheets.
- **Selection:** offices were randomised, with no voluntary withdrawal.
- **Novelty:** results run to nine months, against a control group that also knew a trial was under way.

The comment calls the Varden counter result "the most reliable finding in the literature." The case-processing result comes from the same trial under the same design, and the comment doesn't mention it. A conclusion of "entirely an artifact" has to address that result, and it can't.

**2. The novelty argument turns a suggestion into a conclusion.**
I made a similar point in my Halden review: that the energy decline *looks like* novelty wearing off. That was suggestive, and it remains suggestive. The comment's argument has several problems:
- **Two points don't make a trend.** A straight line through two data points says nothing about the trajectory's shape. Energy could plateau rather than fall to zero.
- **The extrapolation is miscalculated.** Even on the authors' own linear assumption, energy reaches zero at about month 8.7, not month 10.
- **Energy is not output.** The link from self-reported energy to per-hour output is assumed, not shown.
- **The comment contradicts itself.** It concedes that "six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one." That makes durability an open question. Invoking the burden of proof doesn't settle it in either direction.

**3. The meetings section mischaracterises the Varden analysis.**
- The seven offices are the treated half of a pre-specified stratum, not a subgroup chosen after the results were known.
- The meeting data were collected at month six, before the nine-month outcomes existed.
- The Varden authors already said the correlation "cannot establish a mechanism" and registered a confirmatory test.
- Halden's interviews independently reported meeting cuts in 47 of 58 organisations.

The hypothesis is open, with a test pending. "Should not be cited as a mechanism" is right. "Has outrun its evidence" misdescribes how it was reported.

**4. The comment holds different claims to different standards.**
It treats a two-point trend in self-reports as decisive for its own argument, while dismissing a seven-office correlation that was openly labelled exploratory.

**5. The abstract itself escalates.**
It moves from "plausibly a novelty effect" to "entirely an artifact" within two sentences, and the Data note then says the corrected estimates describe only non-random subsets. A defensible conclusion would read something like:

> Measurement and attrition account for roughly half of the reported Halden gain. The remaining ~10% gain per actual hour, in a non-random subset, is of uncertain durability. It is consistent in size with the Varden randomised estimate for non-coverage work.

## Where the evidence now stands, across all three papers

- **Well supported:**
  - Scheduled-hour denominators and manager-reported output both inflate gains substantially.
  - Halden's 23.4% headline does not stand.
  - In coverage-bound work, reduced hours without extra hiring reduce output and service. Varden is randomised, though with only 5 v 5 offices, and Halden's retail figures agree.
- **Moderately supported:** in work not tied to presence, output per actual hour rises by roughly 10–12%, while output per employee is flat to slightly down (about −2% in Varden, about −5% in the Halden subset). Two independent estimates converge here, from a randomised trial and from the corrected pilot.
- **Open:**
  - whether gains persist beyond nine months (Varden's 24-month follow-up)
  - how much attrition biased Halden, which is not yet quantified
  - mechanism, whether rest, process changes or both (Varden's registered test)
  - cost once overtime is counted

I can draft a reply letter to the comment, or a short evidence summary across the three papers.
